causal.conclusion: Two causal contributions are demonstrable: a retrained model validated on overall accuracy only (E8, E19) and shipped to an interface that withheld subgroup reliability for an underrepresented category (E4, E11), and the closing of a subgroup-degradation signal without transmission to the hospital (E12). The treating physician's adoption is a causal contribution (E3, E21) but the foreseeability condition is not met on the facts, so blame for the adoption decision alone is contested.
causal.evidence: S9 sets the test for blameworthiness as wrong-doing, causal contribution, foreseeability and freedom, and holds that foreseeability requires that agents do everything reasonably possible to learn the consequences: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] van de Poel & Royakkers (2011), p. 12: "A person who is held responsible for something must have been able to know the consequences of his or her actions." S4 grounds the control condition that the operator's responsibility shrinks as control shrinks. S1 supplies the warning that causal complexity produces misattribution: [VERBATIM-PAGE-UNVERIFIED] Elish (2019), Abstract: "responsibility for an action may be misattributed to a human actor who had limited control over the behavior of an automated or autonomous system". S6 adds that causation is the wrong level at which to stop: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1065: "the capacity of the different agents, including the users, to make sense of the \"logic\" of the systems' behaviour may be weakened and sometimes lost".

hierarchical.conclusion: What this perspective says that the causal one cannot: the decisive contribution in this case is an unassigned task, not an act. No agent omitted post-deployment verification, because the contract assigns it to no party (E17); the monitoring signal stopped inside the supplier (E12) while the version notice stopped at the technical contact (E13); clinical authority sat with the physician (E16) while the information needed to exercise it sat with the supplier. The causal chain therefore does not identify a culpable node, and it cannot, because the omissions sit at three role handovers rather than inside any single role.
hierarchical.evidence: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1066: "the introduction of AI makes the \"problem of many hands\" more acute". [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Johnson (2020), p. 118: "rotten apples and rotten barrels tend to go together". [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Luegenbiehl & Clancy (2017), p. 84: "it is difficult and, perhaps, unfair to place all the responsibility on individual actors or institutions". S1 documents the resulting pattern, in which the nearest human operator becomes the visible node while control sits elsewhere.

future.conclusion: Forward-looking, three duties are assignable and checkable, and one is not. Assignable: supplier subgroup performance reporting to a named clinical lead (duty A9, authority E12/E13, marker = subgroup report with documented receipt); hospital re-validation before each version goes live (duty A5/A7, authority E17/E16, marker = minuted re-validation by the quality committee); regulator's subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules (duty A11, authority E22/E9-b, marker = published criterion). Not assignable on current facts: the physician's duty to verify the basis of a recommendation, because the interface supplies no subgroup information (E11, E6) and the duty would therefore be unperformable.
future.evidence: S6 defines active responsibility as the forward-looking form and locates the gap in agents who are not sufficiently aware, capable and motivated: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Santoni de Sio & Mecacci (2021), p. 1059: "may not be sufficiently aware, capable, and motivated to see and act according to their moral obligations". S7 requires that control be real, through tracking and tracing conditions, not nominal: [VERBATIM-PAGE-UNVERIFIED] Santoni de Sio & van den Hoven (2018), Abstract: "the system should be able to respond to both the relevant moral reasons of the humans designing and deploying the system". S5 holds that responsibility presupposes capacity and institutional support: [VERIFIED-QUOTE] Reijers et al. (2025), p. 85: "without institutional support, individuals can be blind and lost". S10 supplies the shared, forward-looking dimension.

claims.claim: The v2.1 update causally contributed to the injury: it was validated against overall accuracy only and shipped to a population-level interface for a category underrepresented in the training data, and the option it ranked first was not the clinically indicated choice.
claims.task: Retrain, validate and ship the model together with its interface configuration.
claims.counter: S8 holds that a technology-specific responsibility gap is an assumption rather than a finding, and that ascription to the supplier is unproblematic, so no special causal difficulty exists; the supplier can also argue the physician held the final decision (E5, E16).
claims.reason: Causal contribution rests on E8 (retraining), E19 (assessment basis), E11 (interface) and E21 (ranked option not indicated); the counter addresses ascription, not causation.

claims.claim: Closing the 2023-02-10 subgroup alert without transmitting it is an omission that causally contributed to the physician's non-knowledge at the point of decision.
claims.task: Monitor post-deployment performance and escalate alerts.
claims.counter: The team held no clinical authority and no channel to clinicians (E17); S4 would add that learning behaviour limits predictability, so the omission is organisational rather than individual.
claims.reason: Failure to act counts as causal contribution in S9's account of passive responsibility; the counter redistributes the contribution, it does not remove it.

claims.claim: The adoption of the recommendation is a causal contribution, but the foreseeability condition is not satisfied: the interface carried no subgroup field and no warning (E11), and no reliability information reached the physician (E6, E13).
claims.task: Accept or reject the recommendation and order treatment.
claims.counter: S1 predicts that the nearest operator will absorb blame regardless of control, which is exactly the misattribution to avoid; conversely the physician held a refusal right (E5) and could have asked for the basis of the score, so reasonable effort may have been available.
claims.reason: The fact set records no request for data and no refusal, so the competing readings cannot be separated; the completion marker for the counter-argument (a documented query) does not exist in E1-E22.

claims.claim: The change-assessment rules define the threshold on overall accuracy and specify no subgroup criterion (E22), which is a contributing condition to an unmonitored subgroup decline.
claims.task: Set the evidence standard a change assessment must meet.
claims.counter: Rule content is a legitimate policy choice, and a critic can say the regulator performed no act and no omission in this episode; S3 warns against placing responsibility on institutions for a diffuse causal background.
claims.reason: E22 documents the content of a rule, not conduct in this episode; causation of this injury by the regulator cannot be derived from the facts, and S6's own account warns against legal solutionism.

claims.claim: The IT and quality unit received the v2.1 release note (E13) and had performed acceptance testing at go-live (E17), and no forwarding to clinicians is recorded.
claims.task: Technical acceptance of releases and their internal distribution.
claims.counter: The unit's remit is technical acceptance, not clinical communication (E17), and the note contained no subgroup data in the first place (E13), so causation runs back to A9 rather than through the unit.
claims.reason: A causal chain from the unit to the injury requires a duty to forward clinical content that E17 does not record; the better-supported path is the absence of subgroup content upstream.

claims.claim: The contract assigns installation, updates and pre-deployment acceptance, and assigns post-deployment performance verification to no party (E17); the decisive condition is therefore an unassigned task rather than an individual omission.
claims.task: Allocate post-deployment verification when the system is procured.
claims.counter: S8 would answer that a missing contractual clause is a repairable contractual defect, not a responsibility gap, and that the hospital could have inserted the clause; so this is an ordinary procurement failure.
claims.reason: S6 p. 1066 supports the structural reading and E17 records the omission in the document itself; what the hierarchical reading adds is that no agent can be said to have skipped a task that was never theirs.

claims.claim: Authority to decide is concentrated at the individual level (E16) while the information needed to exercise it is held at the organisational level (E6, E11); the department head received two oral reports and no formal investigation followed (E14).
claims.task: Match decision authority with the information required to use it.
claims.counter: S1's crumple-zone thesis predicts this pattern, but the physician's refusal right (E5) is genuine control, so the mismatch is weaker than in Elish's aviation and nuclear cases; the head's reliance on oral reports is normal practice.
claims.reason: The mismatch is recorded in the facts rather than inferred: E16 allocates final authority to A2, E11 records the missing interface fields, E6 records non-knowledge.

claims.claim: The version notice was routed to the technical contact rather than to clinical staff (E13), while the clearance named a clinical indication (E7, E2); the disclosure channel and the clinical decision channel are separated structurally.
claims.task: Define who receives which document after a version change.
claims.counter: Distribution to a technical contact discharges a contractual notification duty, and S2 notes that accountability routinely sits with leadership while information sits elsewhere, so separation is normal rather than defective.
claims.reason: E13 records both the content and the distribution list, so the separation is a documented fact; the counter explains why it persists, not why it is harmless for a decision-support device.

claims.claim: Hospital administration holds contracting and suspension authority (E16, E17) yet has no technical means to detect subgroup degradation and received no report (E10, E12); formal authority and epistemic access are held by different parties.
claims.task: Exercise contractual leverage to obtain performance evidence.
claims.counter: A critic, and S8, will say that formal authority to suspend plus a contractual right to demand data is sufficient control and that the hospital simply did not exercise it; S3 adds that concentrating fault on one institution is unfair where causes converge.
claims.reason: The fact set records no request for performance data and no refusal, so the counter cannot be excluded; the claim survives only as a description of the authority-access split, not as a finding of failure.

claims.claim: Because the change threshold is defined on overall accuracy (E22), a compliant assessment can record v2.1 as acceptable (E9-b, E19) while a subgroup decline remains invisible; the blind spot is written into the rule, not only into the supplier's conduct.
claims.task: Specify subgroup criteria in the change-assessment framework.
claims.counter: S6 insists that legal and regulatory tools are necessary but not sufficient, and that technical solutionism is a distortion; a critic can add that a rule cannot anticipate every subgroup.
claims.reason: E22 and E19 together show that the same metric governed both the rule and the assessment, which is why no actor departed from the standard and the harm still occurred.

claims.claim: The supplier should carry a forward-looking duty to report subgroup performance to a named clinical lead after every version change; it alone holds the monitoring channel and the distribution list.
claims.task: Subgroup performance reporting after each version change; responsible party A9; authority and resources: owns monitoring output and decides recipients (E12, E13); verifiable completion marker: a subgroup performance report per version with documented receipt by a named clinical lead.
claims.counter: S8 would say this is a disclosure rule that can simply be imposed, not evidence of a responsibility gap; S7's tracing condition is already met because the model is traceable to the ML team, so nothing new is needed.
claims.reason: The duty, the authority and the marker are all anchored in facts; the counter shows the repair is feasible, which is consistent with the claim rather than against it.

claims.claim: The hospital should carry a forward-looking duty to re-validate subgroup performance before each version change goes live; it holds acceptance testing and suspension authority and the internal reporting chain.
claims.task: Re-validate subgroup performance per version; responsible party A5 with A7 executing; authority and resources: acceptance testing (E17), suspension authority (E16), reporting chain (E15, E20); verifiable completion marker: subgroup re-validation minuted by the quality committee before go-live.
claims.counter: Without data access the duty cannot be discharged, so the hospital can plead impossibility; S8 would say the true defect is the absent data-sharing clause, which is a contract term and not a responsibility concept.
claims.reason: The duty is real as a forward-looking assignment but not performable on the current contract (E17); a Contested verdict records that impossibility is a genuine defence and that the repair must include data access.

claims.claim: The physician's forward-looking duty to verify the basis of a recommendation exists but cannot be discharged on the current interface.
claims.task: Verify the basis of a recommendation before acting; responsible party A2; authority and resources: refusal right only (E5), no subgroup information on screen (E11), no reliability notice received (E6, E13); verifiable completion marker: a documented query or refusal logged in the case record where subgroup reliability is unavailable.
claims.counter: S7 requires that control be meaningful rather than nominal, which supports the claim; but S9 requires only reasonable effort, and a documented query was within the physician's power, so the defence is incomplete.
claims.reason: The duty is unperformable as specified, yet an alternative low-cost action existed and is not recorded; the claim is therefore partly supported and partly open.

claims.claim: The regulator should carry a forward-looking duty to include a subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules.
claims.task: Add a subgroup criterion to the change-assessment framework; responsible party A11; authority and resources: rule-making authority over the framework applied to v2.1 (E22, E9-b); verifiable completion marker: a published subgroup criterion against which any change assessment can be checked.
claims.counter: S10 distributes such duties across all connected agents, so singling out the regulator over-weights one node; S3 adds that concentrating responsibility on a single institution is unfair where causes converge.
claims.reason: The duty and the authority are documented, but the burden-sharing between regulator, supplier and hospital is not settled by the facts, so the allocation is contested rather than supported.

claims.claim: The condition that produced the harm is structural and its repair is shared: supplier, hospital, technical unit and regulator all participate in a process that left one subgroup unmonitored, and discharge requires collective action.
claims.task: Joint post-deployment review of subgroup performance across the four organisations.
claims.counter: S10's model was built for global structural injustice and expressly declines to isolate perpetrators; a defendant will say it therefore cannot ground concrete enforceable duties for a licensed device, and S8 will add that no gap has been shown at all.
claims.reason: E17 and E12 show the diffusion directly; the counter limits what the claim can do (it grounds a joint review, not a damages allocation), which is why the claim is stated at that level only.

actorAssessments.cause: None. The patient is the harmed party and made no causal contribution.
actorAssessments.legalReason: No duty was held or breached; the patient is the bearer of the claim, not a candidate for liability.
actorAssessments.nextReason: No forward-looking duty applies, and no authority over system use was held at any point (E1, E3).
actorAssessments.payment: Not applicable: the patient is the claimant, not a payer.

actorAssessments.cause: Adopted the recommendation and administered the treatment (E3, E21).
actorAssessments.legalReason: Causal contribution is present, but foreseeability is not satisfied on the facts: no subgroup field on screen (E11) and no reliability information received (E6, E13). S9 p. 12 sets the standard; whether a documented query was reasonably available is not recorded.
actorAssessments.nextReason: A forward duty to verify the basis of a recommendation is real but not dischargeable on the current interface; the marker would be a logged query or refusal.
actorAssessments.payment: No compensation obligation established on the facts. S2 separates liability, the obligation to compensate, from accountability and blameworthiness, so payment would attach to the organisation unless a professional standard breach is proven.

actorAssessments.cause: Received two oral reports of inconsistent recommendations (E14) and initiated no formal investigation.
actorAssessments.legalReason: A five-month gap separates the reports from the injury (T8, T9), so a preventive path existed in principle; but the reports described inconsistency, not subgroup unreliability, and no written record was made.
actorAssessments.nextReason: A forward duty to convert clinical concerns into a written escalation; authority held is review on request (E16); marker is a dated written referral to the quality committee.
actorAssessments.payment: Not established: payment would fall on the institution rather than on a supervisory role.

actorAssessments.cause: Observed atypical behaviour and reported orally only (E14).
actorAssessments.legalReason: Reporting a concern is consistent with professional duty; no norm violation is recorded.
actorAssessments.nextReason: A forward duty to record concerns in writing exists; no authority to suspend use was held; marker is a written concern entry with date.

actorAssessments.cause: Operated the system, held the reporting chain, and received neither validation report nor monitoring alert (E10, E12).
actorAssessments.legalReason: The contract assigns post-deployment verification to no party (E17), which supports the hospital's position; against that, it held suspension authority (E16) and had received release information (E13). S2 treats the liable party as usually the organisation in which the mishap occurred.
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to re-validate subgroup performance per version and to secure data access by contract; marker is a minuted re-validation before go-live.
actorAssessments.payment: Contested: primary candidate for a compensation obligation under S2's liability notion, contested by the absence of an assigned verification duty.

actorAssessments.cause: Reviewed the event only after it occurred (E20, E21); no causal role before it.
actorAssessments.legalReason: Post-event review was performed on the facts recorded; no prior report reached the committee (E10, E12, E14).
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to require subgroup evidence as a condition of continued system use; authority is system-level review (E16); marker is a standing pre-condition minuted per version.

actorAssessments.cause: Performed acceptance testing at go-live (E17) and received the v2.1 notice without forwarding it (E13).
actorAssessments.legalReason: The unit acted within its technical remit, and the notice contained no subgroup data to forward; against that, a version change on a live clinical device went unreported to users for five months and twelve days (E13).
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to route version changes to clinical leads as well as to systems; authority over the distribution list is shared with A9; marker is a forwarding log with clinical acknowledgement.
actorAssessments.payment: Not established: no contracting capacity, so payment would attach to the institution.

actorAssessments.cause: Held contracting and suspension authority and signed a contract with no verification clause (E17).
actorAssessments.legalReason: Signature of the contract is a documented act, but no norm requiring a verification clause is recorded in the facts; the omission is shared with A9, which also signed.
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to allocate post-deployment verification in the contract and to exercise suspension leverage; marker is an executed contract amendment naming an owner and a reporting cadence.
actorAssessments.payment: Contested: liable as the contracting party for the institution, subject to product-liability allocation against A9.

actorAssessments.cause: Retrained and shipped v2.1 validated on overall accuracy only (E8, E19), closed a subgroup alert (E12), and issued a notice with no subgroup data to a technical contact (E13).
actorAssessments.legalReason: The supplier held knowledge (E4, E12, E19), the monitoring channel and the distribution list, and the shipped interface withheld subgroup reliability (E11). S2's liability notion, the obligation to compensate for harm done, points to this party; the page for that definition is not verifiable from the text layer.
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to report subgroup performance per version to a named clinical lead; marker is a report with documented receipt; authority held is sufficient (E12, E13).
actorAssessments.payment: Supported: the party with the strongest claim to a compensation obligation, subject to contract terms and product-liability rules.

actorAssessments.cause: Recorded the subgroup decline on 2023-02-10 and closed the alert without escalation (E12); ran the assessment on overall accuracy (E19).
actorAssessments.legalReason: The team holds no contracting capacity and no obligation to the patient directly; liability would attach to the employer (A9), while the team's exposure is professional rather than legal.
actorAssessments.nextReason: Forward duty to escalate any subgroup metric below protocol threshold; authority over monitoring is sufficient; marker is an escalation ticket with a named recipient outside the team.
actorAssessments.payment: Not established: no capacity to pay, and no direct duty to the injured party is recorded.

actorAssessments.cause: Administered a framework whose threshold is overall accuracy with no subgroup criterion (E22); no knowledge of v2.1 is recorded under the adopted branch (E9-b).
actorAssessments.legalReason: No act or omission touching this patient is recorded; the clearance covered v1.0 (E7) and the change fell within the framework as written (E9-b, E22).
actorAssessments.nextReason: A forward duty to add a subgroup criterion is arguable, but S10 distributes it across connected agents and S3 warns against concentrating responsibility on one institution.
actorAssessments.payment: Not established: no liability path is recorded in the facts.

actorAssessments.cause: Produced a recommendation whose first-ranked option the review record states was not clinically indicated (E21), through an interface with no subgroup field or warning banner (E11).
actorAssessments.legalReason: A technical system holds no duty, capacity or liability; its conduct is attributed to the humans who designed, validated and deployed it.
actorAssessments.nextReason: No forward-looking duty can attach to an artefact; the assignable duties are those of A9, A10, A5, A7 and A11.

caseFields.answer1: The injury traces to four documented conditions rather than to one act: a retrained model validated against overall accuracy only (E8, E19); an interface that displayed a population-level score with no subgroup field and no warning banner (E11); a subgroup decline recorded internally and closed without transmission (E12); and a version change that reached clinical staff only after five months and twelve days (E13). The recommendation's first-ranked option was, per the post-event review, not clinically indicated (E21), within the approved indication (E18, E7). Responsibility is distributed by function: epistemic and disclosure authority with the supplier (A9, A10), deployment and suspension authority with the hospital (A5, A8, A7), decision authority with the physician (A2, E16), and rule authority with the regulator (A11, E22). No party was assigned post-deployment verification (E17).
caseFields.answer4: A gap may exist, and it is narrow. On S6's four-way division: the culpability gap is not established here, because the supplier's knowledge (E4, E12, E19) and the interface design (E11) satisfy the foreseeability and control conditions that S9 p. 12 sets, so blame has a fitting target. The moral accountability gap is partially present, since the physician could not explain the basis of the score to the patient (E6, E11; S6 p. 1065). The public accountability gap is not examined on these facts. The active responsibility gap is present and is the one that matters: the duty to verify subgroup performance after deployment belonged to no party (E17), the monitoring output was held by one party and the clinical decision by another (E12, E16), and the physician's verification duty was unperformable on the interface supplied (E11, E6).
caseFields.answer5: Repair the allocation, not the technology. Three assignments, each with an owner, the authority to perform it, and a checkable marker: (1) supplier subgroup performance reporting per version to a named clinical lead, marker a report with documented receipt; (2) hospital re-validation of subgroup performance before each version goes live, marker a quality-committee minute, with data access secured by contract amendment; (3) a subgroup criterion in the change-assessment rules, marker a published criterion against which any assessment can be checked. Add one interface change: display training-sample size and a low-sample warning for the patient's category, which is what makes the physician's forward duty performable at all.
caseFields.comparison: Causal identifies two contributions (C1, C2) and one contested one (C3), but cannot say why no agent's contribution was decisive. Hierarchical answers that: the decisive condition is an unassigned task at three handovers (C6, C7, C8), which is why a search for a culpable node returns either the nearest human (S1) or nobody (S6 p. 1066). It adds the location of the omission and the authority-access split (C9, C10); it does not add a culpable party. Forward-looking adds what both lack: an owner per task, the authority to perform it, and a marker that can be audited (C11-C15). Its limit is stated in C12 and C13: two of the duties are not performable on the current contract and interface, so the gap cannot be closed by exhortation.
caseFields.conclusion: The case is not one of a rogue algorithm or a negligent physician. A cleared device was updated under a rule that measured only overall accuracy, monitoring detected the subgroup decline and did not pass it on, the version notice did not reach clinicians, and no party was contractually assigned post-deployment verification. The accountable party is identifiable, the compensation obligation most plausibly falls on the supplier, and the responsibility gap lies in forward-looking duty allocation rather than in culpability.
caseFields.gapTask: Assign and perform post-deployment subgroup performance verification and disclosure after every model version change, and make the resulting evidence available at the point of clinical decision.
caseFields.gapMechanism: Many hands (responsibility diffused across contract, monitoring and disclosure handovers)
caseFields.gapPeople: A9 system supplier; A10 supplier ML team; A5 hospital; A7 hospital IT/quality unit; A11 regulatory authority
caseFields.gapReason: The gap is in S6's fourth category, active responsibility, not in culpability: the supplier knew (E4, E12, E19) and the physician did not (E6), which is the pattern S6 p. 1059 describes for agents who are not sufficiently aware, capable and motivated. Mechanism is recorded as the closest available value because the omission is distributed across a contractual handover (E17), an internal handover (E12) and a disclosure handover (E13); if the dropdown offers a value naming diffusion or organisational black boxes, that value fits better and should replace this one. Stage is recorded as validation/testing because the omitted act is post-deployment re-validation; if a post-deployment monitoring value exists it is more precise. Counter-argument that no gap exists, and the response: S8 argues that a technology-specific responsibility gap is a prevailing assumption rather than a finding, that responsibility is a flexible practice, and that every element here is ascribable, which by itself shows there is no gap; S4's founding argument is also narrower than the case, since it turns on unpredictability that learning creates. The response is that this counter is correct about culpability and does not reach the gap claimed here: the gap is not that nobody can be blamed, but that the task which would have prevented the harm was assigned to nobody (E17), so no agent departed from any standard and every agent can point to a rule it followed (E19, E22, E9-b). That is S6's many hands point at p. 1066 rather than an unpredictability claim, and it survives S8's objection because it is an allocation finding, not a blame finding.
caseFields.repair: Contract amendment naming an owner for post-deployment subgroup verification and granting the hospital access to subgroup performance data; a standing requirement that no version goes live without a minuted subgroup re-validation; supplier reporting of subgroup performance per version to a named clinical lead with documented receipt; a subgroup criterion added to the change-assessment rules (E22); interface change displaying training-sample size and a low-sample warning for the patient's category.
caseFields.gapCheck: Verification of the repair: (a) contract text naming the owner and a reporting cadence; (b) a quality-committee minute per version, dated before go-live; (c) a subgroup report per version with a receipt record naming the clinical lead; (d) a published subgroup criterion in the change-assessment framework; (e) an audit showing no version entered clinical use without items (b) and (c). Absence of any one of these is a checkable failure of the repair, which is what distinguishes the repair from an aspiration.
